I assume that you're doing body-weight squats. (ie without additional weight such as a barbell or dumbells.)

  • You want to stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart, and then point the toes slightly outward.

  • Next, squat down, with your knees tracking over your feet the whole way.

  • Get your ass to the grass. Go low, as though you're about to drop a deuce in the woods. Such as how you've seen people from Asian countries sitting. http://www.eveandersson.com/photos/china/beijing-wangfujing-men-squatting-large.jpg

  • Use that little bit of 'bounce' at the bottom of the movement to help you stand back up.

The movement is essentially the same with weight, but before attempting a weighted squat, I strongly suggest that you watch the following videos:

1) Mark Rippetoe:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QhVC_AnZYYM

2) Alan Thrall:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bs_Ej32IYgo

3) Mehdi from Stronglifts 5x5:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VnV7vEi7Sz8

Most people bitch and complain about Squatting and leg-day in general, but I assure you that the squat is the ultimate strength-training movement. Properly performed, it works nearly every muscular system in the body. If you want to get strong, I highly recommend following the Stronglifts 5x5 program and then transitioning into the Madcow 5x5 program (google it) once you max out the gains from Stronglifts (about 9 months to a year). Starting as a novice lifter, I have used Stronglifts/Madcow to bring my squat from 45 lbs (the empty bar) to a personal best of 365 lbs x 3 reps. Took me about a year.

Form is the ultimate consideration. It is much much better to lift a lesser weight with good form, than to hurt yourself showing off at a higher weight. With bad form you can hurt yourself badly. Watch the videos.

I'll stir things a bit:

  • You shouldn't necessarily keep your feet about shoulder width or point your toes outwards; the point is to find the position that allows you to squat as deep as possible, as comfortable as possible, and this depends on your body shape, however for the huge majority of people shoulder width with toes pointed outwards slightly is ideal. I'm pointing this out, because if this setup is not comfortable for you, you should alter it.
  • Squat down as deep as you can, without your heels being pulled up; this might not be ass to grass, but at the bare minimum your thighs should reach a position where they are parallel to the floor.
  • You have to do the 'bounce' right or it will hurt your knee; according to Rippetoe (I don't bounce so I don't have first hand experience) the bounce does not involves the knee, only the hips; this is a special time when you should make sure the knees are over your feet and do not travel forward, and correctly pushing the hips back will prevent this.
  • Feet must point in the same direction as your knees.
  • The force should go through the heel, not the balls of your feet.
  • You should work on flexibility until you can squat ass to grass, with feet pointed forward. If you do squats regularly up to your limit, first regarding how deep and later about how straight your feet are, this will happen on it's own eventually, but targeted flexibility work will get you there faster.
  • Shaking a little bit at your legs or knees, due to lack of strength or being tired, is okay, as long as your knees are over your feet, and pointing in the same direction as your feet.
  • If you still have pain, despite your knees being kept over your feet, and knees pointing in the same direction as your feet, from doing a few (say, about 5 or less) squats, or the pain remains after you stop squatting, see a doctor. If you get pain, no matter what the conditions triggering the pain are, STOP.

This is an excellent addendum to my comment. Thanks @Coz for contributing additional information.

Edit: anyone helping others to squat with good form is tops in my book!

If your knees are hurting, you might be doing the squat wrong. When you squat, do your knees go forward or do they stay in place? If they go forward, you're doing it wrong. When they go forward, you're just putting pressure on your knees which causes the pain. When you keep your knees still and stick your ass back, you won't have the knee pain and you'll feel your muscles work.

On the more lighthearted side, dark rides are also used for attractions that are more oriented toward fun, comedy, or 'edutainment'.
